assumptions: The founder begins with paid commissioning analytics rather than underwriting risk directly.
A licensed insurer, not the founder, ultimately carries regulated performance risk.
The family installer grants only voluntary, consented pilot access.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A consented cohort showing buyers pay for prediction or protection, stable weather-normalized loss curves, acceptable claim attribution, signed installer distribution, and an insurer term sheet with economics that preserve attractive contribution margin.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Turning uncertain installed performance into a measured outcome is a coherent response to a real trust barrier, but demand specifically for paid protection is not established.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: High purchase cost and disappointing operating outcomes create meaningful pain, yet no evidence shows owners, installers, or lenders will pay the proposed fees for a weather-normalized guarantee.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Upfront analytics and recurring cover offer useful cash-flow shapes, but loss ratios, reserves, channel shares, servicing costs, claims frequency, retention, and fully loaded margins remain unknown.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish installations through a small set of cooperative installers form a testable beachhead within a growing installed base, although the realistically insurable subset is unclear.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A focused Polish performance dataset could support a niche position, but OEMs, installers, utilities, and insurers own stronger channels and can add similar protection.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Credible loss data could extend into lender underwriting, installer scoring, housing portfolios, diagnostics, and other electrified-building assets.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Longitudinal installation and claims data could compound, but no data rights, exclusive channel, guarantee book, or durable access currently exists.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Independent measured-outcome protection is materially stronger than a basic equipment warranty when attribution is credible, but behavior, weather, and tariffs make that promise difficult to trust.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Heat-pump deployment, installer-quality concerns, and a growing installed base support timely experimentation despite policy and financing volatility.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer enables a consented pilot and installers or lenders offer point-of-sale reach, but channel agreements and customer ownership are unproven and conflicts are plausible.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Analytics are feasible part-time, but regulated risk transfer, actuarial credibility, telemetry consent, adverse selection, reserves, and claims disputes require capabilities well beyond a solo launch.

highest_value_structural_change: Secure an insurer-backed, standardized guarantee plus multi-installer telemetry rights so the business controls the performance dataset and customer-facing measurement layer without retaining balance-sheet risk.
main_structural_strength: A measurable outcome product can create recurring revenue and a proprietary installation-performance dataset from a large emerging asset base.
primary_score_limiter: The core guarantee economics and legal structure cannot be assessed without loss history, risk capacity, and evidence of payer demand.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Performance is strongly affected by occupant behavior, weather, and tariffs, while regulated risk transfer may require an authorized insurer and substantial reserves.
